claim: C/EBPα is composed of a bZip DNA-binding domain on its C-terminus and a tripartite transactivation domain on its N-terminus.
source: C/EBPα is composed of a bZip DNA-binding domain on its C-terminus and a tripartite transactivation domain on its N-terminus (Figure 1B; Ramberger et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramberger et al., 2021b and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: During hematopoiesis, C/EBPα is most highly expressed in granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (GMPs).
source: During hematopoiesis, it is most highly expressed in granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (GMPs) (Ohlsson et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ohlsson et al., 2016.

claim: The absence of C/EBPα inhibits the formation of GMPs and monocytes/macrophages.
source: its absence inhibits the formation of GMPs, and monocytes/macrophages (Heath et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heath et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2004.

claim: C/EBPα-induced BMT requires partnership with the transcription factor PU.1.
source: The C/EBPα-induced BMT requires partnership with the TF PU.1, which participates in regulatory networks of both B/T cells and in myeloid cells (Rothenberg, 2014; Laiosa et al., 2006; Heinz et al., 2010; Arinobu et al., 2007; Leddin et al., 2011; Singh et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PU.1 participates in regulatory networks of both B/T cells and myeloid cells.
source: The C/EBPα-induced BMT requires partnership with the TF PU.1, which participates in regulatory networks of both B/T cells and in myeloid cells (Rothenberg, 2014; Laiosa et al., 2006; Heinz et al., 2010; Arinobu et al., 2007; Leddin et al., 2011; Singh et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: C/EBPαR35A recapitulated the phenotype induced by C/EBPα3RA, while R12A and R86A essentially displayed no effect.
source: Results showed that C/EBPαR35A recapitulated the phenotype induced by C/EBPα, while R12A and R86A essentially displayed no effect (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: R35A cells induced for 120 hr resembled normal macrophages, showing extensive F-actin filaments and eccentric nuclei, as well as high phagocytic capacity.
source: R35A cells induced for 120 hr resembled normal macrophages, showing extensive F-actin filaments and eccentric nuclei, as well as high phagocytic capacity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Replacing arginine 35 with alanine in C/EBPα dramatically increases the speed of induced BMT.
source: These findings indicate that replacing arginine 35 with alanine in C/EBPα dramatically increases the speed of induced BMT, generating macrophage-like cells similar to those obtained with the wild-type.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results described in the preceding text.

claim: At 1 hpi, the gene expression patterns in C/EBPαR35A-infected cells were similar to those of 18 hpi wild-type-infected cells.
source: At just 1 hpi, the gene expression patterns in C/EBPαR35A-infected cells were similar to those of 18 hpi wild-type-infected cells, reaching similar expression levels at 120 hpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The largest differences in gene expression between the wild-type and mutant cells were observed between 0 and 1 hpi.
source: The largest differences in gene expression between the wild-type and mutant cells were observed between 0 and 1 hpi (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Clusters I and II were enriched for macrophage-myeloid-related Gene Ontology (GO) terms and included the myeloid genes Itgam, Lyz2, Csf1r, and Cd14.
source: Clusters I and II were enriched for macrophage-myeloid-related Gene Ontology (GO) terms and included the myeloid genes Itgam, Lyz2, Csf1r, and Cd14 (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis and data shown in figures.

claim: Cluster VII was enriched for B cell-related GO terms and included the B cell genes Cd19, Pax5, Ebf1, and Rag2.
source: On the other hand, cluster VII was enriched for B cell-related GO terms and included the B cell genes Cd19, Pax5, Ebf1, and Rag2 (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis and data shown in figures.

claim: The analysis identified 91,830 regions that showed significant differences in chromatin accessibility throughout wild-type- or mutant-induced BMT.
source: Our analysis identified 91,830 regions that showed significant differences in chromatin accessibility throughout wild-type- or mutant-induced BMT, representing in their vast majority TF-bound GREs (Buenrostro et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis and a citation to Buenrostro et al., 2015.

claim: PCA of the differential ATAC peaks confirmed the acceleration of chromatin accessibility changes by C/EBPαR35A, with the coordinates of the 1–6 hpi C/EBPαR35A samples resembling those of the 18 hpi C/EBPαWT sample.
source: PCA of the differential ATAC peaks further confirmed the acceleration of chromatin accessibility changes by C/EBPαR35A, with the coordinates of the 1–6 hpi C/EBPαR35A samples resembling those of the 18 hpi C/EBPαWT sample (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: C/EBPαR35A already initiated chromatin opening at promoters and enhancers of Itgam and Lyz2 within 1 hpi, and this increased over time much more rapidly than with C/EBPαWT cells.
source: C/EBPαR35A already initiated chromatin opening at promoters and enhancers of Itgam and Lyz2 within 1 hpi, and this increased over time much more rapidly than with C/EBPαWT cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: While mutant-induced changes occurred already at 1 hpi and progressed from there onward, the same sites showed a transient chromatin opening in wild-type-induced cells.
source: Strikingly, however, as exemplified for Cd19 and Pax5, while mutant-induced changes occurred already at 1 hpi and progressed from there onward, the same sites showed a transient chromatin opening in wild-type-induced cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) revealed no significant differences in overall DNA binding affinities between C/EBPαWT and C/EBPαR35A.
source: An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) revealed no significant differences in overall DNA binding affinities between the two C/EBPα forms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Faster and transiently opening GREs were enriched for AP-1/leucine zipper family TF motifs (c-Fos, c-Jun, and JunB), known to heterodimerize with C/EBPα and activate myeloid genes.
source: Results in Figure 3A showed that faster and transiently opening GREs were enriched for AP-1/leucine zipper family TF motifs (c-Fos, c-Jun, and JunB), known to heterodimerize with C/EBPα and activate myeloid genes (Cai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 3A and a citation to Cai et al., 2008.

claim: Faster closing GREs were mostly enriched for ETS family TF motifs (Ets1, Fli1, SpiB, and Gabpa), linked to B cell lineage differentiation and function.
source: In contrast, faster closing GREs were mostly enriched for ETS family TF motifs (Ets1, Fli1, SpiB, and Gabpa), linked to B cell lineage differentiation and function (Eyquem et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2001; Xue et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis and citations to Eyquem et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2001; Xue et al., 2007.

claim: The Spi1 (PU.1) motif was enriched in both the accelerated chromatin opening and closing groups.
source: Of note, the Spi1 (PU.1) motif was enriched in both the accelerated chromatin opening and closing groups (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), possibly reflecting the known dual roles of PU.1 in B cells and macrophages (Scott et al., 1994; Singh et al., 1999; Heinz et al., 2010; Rothenberg, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis shown in figures and citations.

claim: C/EBPαR35A preferentially interacted with Spi1 (PU.1), showing a 3.6-fold increase in biotin label compared to C/EBPαWT.
source: A comparison of the high confidence C/EBPαWT and C/EBPαR35A interactome revealed that C/EBPαR35A preferentially interacted with Spi1 (PU.1), showing a 3.6-fold increase in biotin label compared to C/EBPαWT.
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-dependent biotin identification assay data.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed an approximately twofold increase in the interaction between C/EBPαR35A and PU.1 compared to C/EBPαWT and PU.1.
source: The results showed an approximately twofold increase in the interaction between C/EBPαR35A and PU.1 compared to C/EBPαWT and PU.1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Proximity ligation assay showed a significantly higher number of fluorescent nuclear dots for the combination of C/EBPαR35A with PU.1 than with C/EBPαWT.
source: Finally, performing a proximity ligation assay (PLA) to study the protein's interaction in live cells showed a significantly higher number of fluorescent nuclear dots for the combination of C/EBPαR35A with PU.1 than with C/EBPαWT (Figure 3D), again indicating a higher affinity between the two proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the presence of PU.1, C/EBPαR35A activated Mac-1 more strongly than C/EBPαWT.
source: The results showed that in the presence of PU.1, C/EBPαR35A activated Mac-1 more strongly than C/EBPαWT, while cells infected with PU.1 only showed weak Mac-1 activation and C/EBPα only cells remained negative (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells co-expressing C/EBPαR35A and PU.1 displayed more striking morphological changes than those with C/EBPαWT and PU.1.
source: Additionally, cells co-expressing C/EBPαR35A and PU.1 displayed more striking morphological changes than those with C/EBPαWT and PU.1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: C/EBPαR35A exhibits a similar stability than wild-type protein and under steady-state condition is expressed at 20–30% lower levels.
source: Cycloheximide treatment experiments showed that C/EBPαR35A exhibits a similar stability than wild-type protein and under steady-state condition is expressed at 20–30% lower levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cycloheximide treatment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: C/EBPαR35A-Halo cells co-expressing PU.1 showed a substantially decreased interaction with LoMC and increased interaction with HiMC at 6 hpi.
source: In contrast, C/EBPαR35A-Halo cells co-expressing PU.1 showed a substantially decreased interaction with LoMC and increased interaction with HiMC, while PU.1 only moderately affected the distribution of C/EBPαWT-Halo particles (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: At 24 hpi, both forms of C/EBPα showed decreased interaction with LoMC and increased interaction with HiMC, although the differential effects of PU.1 co-expression were milder than at 6 hpi.
source: At 24 hpi, both forms of C/EBPα showed decreased interaction with LoMC and increased interaction with HiMC, although the differential effects of PU.1 co-expression were milder than at 6 hpi (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: PU.1 binds to four sites 50–150 kb upstream of Cyfip2 in B cells but is essentially absent at these sites in macrophages.
source: Mining of published data (Mullen et al., 2011) showed that PU.1 binds to four sites 50–150 kb upstream of Cyfip2 in B cells but is essentially absent at these sites in macrophages (highlighted in red).
evidence: This claim is supported by mining of published data from Mullen et al., 2011.

claim: Both PU.1 and C/EBPα bind to the promoter of Havcr2 and three additional GREs in macrophages but not in B cells.
source: Conversely, both PU.1 and C/EBPα bind to the promoter of Havcr2 and three additional GREs in macrophages but not in B cells (highlighted in green, Figure 5C), showing that PU.1 can bind to both B- and M-GREs while C/EBPα can only bind to M-GREs.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At 3 hpi, PU.1 showed higher occupancy at the B-GREs of C/EBPαWT cells and a modestly increased binding at the M-GREs of C/EBPαR35A cells.
source: Analyzing the PU.1 binding sites in primary B cells induced by C/EBPα for 3 hr, the factor showed higher occupancy at the B-GREs of C/EBPαWT cells and a modestly increased binding at the M-GREs of C/EBPαR35A cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: C/EBPαWT strongly bound to the B-GREs and weakly to the M-GREs, while C/EBPαR35A was selectively bound at the M-GREs.
source: Similarly, C/EBPαWT strongly bound to the B-GREs and weakly to the M-GREs, while C/EBPαR35A was selectively bound at the M-GREs (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: C/EBPαWT triggered a transient and partial opening of B-GREs at 1 hpi and closure at 18 hpi, while the mutant induced an immediate and progressive closure.
source: Notably, while C/EBPαWT triggered a transient and partial opening of B-GREs at 1 hpi and closure at 18 hpi, the mutant induced an immediate and progressive closure (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The majority of the observed 1647 sites that were bound Less by PU.1 became inaccessible at 18 hpi in C/EBPαWT cells, showing a transient opening between 1 and 6 hpi.
source: As seen from the ATAC-seq data, the majority of the observed 1647 sites that were bound Less by PU.1 became inaccessible at 18 hpi in C/EBPαWT cells, showing a transient opening between 1 and 6 hpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: In C/EBPαR35A cells, sites bound Less by PU.1 became already partially closed at 1 hpi and fully inaccessible after 18 hpi.
source: In contrast, in C/EBPαR35A cells these sites became already partially closed at 1 hpi and fully inaccessible after 18 hpi (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For the 2650 sites bound More by PU.1, chromatin accessibility increased already at 1 hpi in the mutant cells, while in wild-type cells they only opened at 120 hpi.
source: The opposite was observed for the 2650 sites bound More by PU.1, where chromatin accessibility increased already at 1 hpi in the mutant cells, while in wild-type cells they only opened at 120 hpi (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Genes associated to sites bound Less by PU.1 showed a strong enrichment of B cell-related GO terms while More-bound sites were enriched for myeloid-related GO terms.
source: As predicted, genes associated to sites bound Less by PU.1 showed a strong enrichment of B cell-related GO terms while More-bound sites were enriched for myeloid-related GO terms (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Of 7144 differentially occupied sites, 4352 sites were bound Less by C/EBPαR35A.
source: Of 7144 differentially occupied sites, 4352 sites were bound Less by C/EBPαR35A.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Approximately 70% of sites bound Less by C/EBPαR35A started closing at 1 hpi in C/EBPαR35A cells while in C/EBPαWT cells they only closed at 120 hpi, after transiently opening between 1 and 6 hpi.
source: Approximately 70% of these started closing at 1 hpi in C/EBPαR35A cells while in C/EBPαWT cells they only closed at 120 hpi, after transiently opening between 1 and 6 hpi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 783 sites were bound Less by both PU.1 and C/EBPαR35A, whereas 385 sites were bound More by both PU.1 and mutant C/EBPα.
source: Finally, we tested sites bound Less by both PU.1 and C/EBPαR35A and found 783 shared sites, whereas 385 sites were bound More by both PU.1 and mutant C/EBPα.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: No overlap was found between PU.1 bound Less and C/EBPα bound More or vice versa.
source: In contrast, no overlap was found between PU.1 bound Less and C/EBPα bound More or vice versa (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) showing a strong positive correlation in the binding of the two factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by genome-wide ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PCA of the data showed an accelerated BMT time course of gene expression and chromatin accessibility (ATAC peaks) for the C/EBPαR35K-induced cells.
source: PCA of the data showed an accelerated BMT time course of gene expression and chromatin accessibility (ATAC peaks) for the C/EBPαR35K-induced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), similar but not identical to those seen with C/EBPαR35A cells (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: After treating BLaER2 cells with 4-OHT for 24 hr and immunoprecipitating C/EBPα followed by western blotting and staining with an antibody specific for asymmetrically di-methylated arginine-containing proteins, C/EBPα could be detected in BLaER2 but not in BlaER2-A cells.
source: After treating the cells with 4-OHT for 24 hr and immunoprecipitating C/EBPα followed by western blotting and staining of the blot with an antibody specific for asymmetrically di-methylated arginine-containing proteins, C/EBPα could be detected in BLaER2 but not in BlaER2-A cells, as expected (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Similar results were obtained with transfected 293T cells, showing methylated C/EBPα in the wild-type but not mutant cells.
source: Similar results were obtained with transfected 293T cells, showing methylated C/EBPα in the wild-type but not mutant cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Only Carm1 induced asymmetric di-methylation of C/EBPα and this was restricted to the wild-type protein.
source: Only Carm1 induced asymmetric di-methylation of C/EBPα (as detected with an antibody specific for the modification) and that this was restricted to the wild-type protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-transfection and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Both C/EBPαWT and C/EBPαR35A are capable of interacting with Carm1.
source: We next performed Co-IP experiments to examine whether C/EBPα and Carm1 can interact, using 293T cells co-transfected with the two proteins, and found that both C/EBPαWT and C/EBPαR35A are capable of interacting with Carm1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Only the peptide containing arginine 35 generated a signal in the in vitro methylation assay using 14 synthetic peptides spanning the entire C/EBPα molecule.
source: To determine which of the 20 arginines in C/EBPα can be bound by Carm1, we conducted an in vitro methylation assay using 14 synthetic peptides spanning the entire molecule. Only the peptide containing arginine 35 generated a signal (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro methylation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Only unmethylated R35 peptide could be methylated by Carm1, with all other conditions being negative.
source: The three peptides were then treated with purified Carm1, Prmt1, Prmt3, Prmt6, or Prmt8 proteins. Only unmethylated R35 peptide could be methylated Carm1, with all other conditions being negative (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro methylation assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: PU.1 interacts more strongly with the unmethylated peptide than with the asymmetrically di-methylated R35 peptide.
source: The comparison of a 15 mer with either an unmethylated or an asymmetrically di-methylated R35 showed that PU.1 interacts more strongly with the unmethylated peptide (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRISMA analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Carm1 overexpression resulted in a delay of both Mac-1 activation and Cd19 silencing in 4-OHT-induced wild-type but not mutant C/EBPα-containing cells.
source: Carm1 overexpression resulted in a delay of both Mac-1 activation and Cd19 silencing in 4-OHT-induced wild-type but not mutant C/EBPα-containing cells (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Treatment of 4-OHT-induced C/EBPαWT-expressing cells with TP064 resulted in a robust acceleration of both Mac-1 upregulation and Cd19 silencing while the kinetics of C/EBPαR35A-expressing RAC1 cells were not altered.
source: Conversely, treatment of 4-OHT-induced C/EBPαWT-expressing cells with TP064 resulted in a robust acceleration of both Mac-1 upregulation and Cd19 silencing while the kinetics of C/EBPαR35A-expressing RAC1 cells were not altered (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Cells with the lowest Carm1 levels transitioned to a macrophage-like identity faster than those with higher levels, with the most substantial differences occurring during the early timepoints.
source: This showed that cells with the lowest Carm1 levels transitioned to a macrophage-like identity faster than those with higher levels, with the most substantial differences occurring during the early timepoints (Figure 7H), reflecting the more pronounced acceleration of gene expression within the first hours after induction of C/EBPαR35A (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell gene expression data analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Examining the expression of Carm1 in CMPs, GMPs, granulocytes, and macrophages revealed a steady decrease during differentiation.
source: Examining the expression of Carm1 in CMPs, GMPs, granulocytes, and macrophages (Choi et al., 2019) revealed a steady decrease during differentiation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Choi et al., 2019.

claim: The highest Carm1 activity was detected in GMPs, with a 3.5-fold decrease in granulocytes and a further 4.5-fold decrease in monocytes.
source: The highest Carm1 activity was detected in GMPs, with a 3.5-fold decrease in granulocytes and a further 4.5-fold decrease in monocytes (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data measuring AsDM-BAF155 shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GMPs seeded in semisolid medium containing TP064 showed a significant dose-dependent reduction of granulocyte colonies and a corresponding increase in monocyte colonies.
source: The results showed a significant dose-dependent reduction of granulocyte colonies and a corresponding increase in monocyte colonies (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony forming assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The observed bias in colony types was not due to a granulocyte-specific toxicity of the inhibitor, as the total number of colonies remained unchanged.
source: The observed bias was not due to a granulocyte-specific toxicity of the inhibitor, as the total number of colonies remained unchanged (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony forming assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treatment of RAW 264.7 cells with TP064 showed a four- to fivefold increase in the number of nuclear dots in a PLA using antibodies against C/EBPα and PU.1.
source: Our results showed a four- to fivefold increase in the number of nuclear dots in treated compared to untreated cells (Figure 8D), indicating that the inhibition of methylation of endogenous C/EBPα increased the factor's affinity for interaction with PU.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: C/EBPα and PU.1 are expressed at similar levels in TP064-treated and untreated RAW cells.
source: The finding that C/EBPα and PU.1 are expressed at similar levels in treated and untreated cells indicates that the inhibitor does not alter the proteins' expression and thus could not explain the observed PLA differences (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Incoming C/EBPα binds to PU.1, an obligate partner expressed in B cells, leading to the release of PU.1 from B cell enhancers, chromatin closing and silencing of the B cell program.
source: Thus, incoming C/EBPα binds to PU.1, an obligate partner expressed in B cells, leading to the release of PU.1 from B cell enhancers, chromatin closing and silencing of the B cell program.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the mechanism described in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Released PU.1 redistributes to macrophage enhancers newly occupied by C/EBPα, causing chromatin opening and activation of macrophage genes.
source: Released PU.1 redistributes to macrophage enhancers newly occupied by C/EBPα, causing chromatin opening and activation of macrophage genes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the mechanism described in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: All these steps are accelerated by C/EBPαR35A, initiated by its increased affinity for PU.1.
source: All these steps are accelerated by C/EBPαR35A, initiated by its increased affinity for PU.1.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the mechanism described in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Wild-type C/EBPα is methylated by Carm1 at arginine 35.
source: Wild-type C/EBPα is methylated by Carm1 at arginine 35 and the enzyme's perturbations modulate BMT velocity as predicted from the observations with the mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental findings including immunoprecipitation, western blotting, and in vitro methylation assays.

claim: Perturbations of Carm1 modulate BMT velocity as predicted from the observations with the mutant.
source: Wild-type C/EBPα is methylated by Carm1 at arginine 35 and the enzyme's perturbations modulate BMT velocity as predicted from the observations with the mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by Carm1 gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Increasing the proportion of unmethylated C/EBPα in granulocyte/macrophage progenitors by inhibiting Carm1 biases the cell's differentiation toward macrophages.
source: Increasing the proportion of unmethylated C/EBPα in granulocyte/macrophage progenitors by inhibiting Carm1 biases the cell's differentiation toward macrophages, suggesting that cell fate decision velocity and lineage directionality are closely linked processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by colony forming assay data with GMPs treated with Carm1 inhibitor.

claim: Cell fate decision velocity and lineage directionality are closely linked processes.
source: Increasing the proportion of unmethylated C/EBPα in granulocyte/macrophage progenitors by inhibiting Carm1 biases the cell's differentiation toward macrophages, suggesting that cell fate decision velocity and lineage directionality are closely linked processes.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the GMP differentiation experiments.

claim: Lineage-restricted transcription factors play a crucial role in driving cell differentiation by repressing the old gene expression program while activating new ones at bifurcation points.
source: It is widely accepted that lineage-restricted transcription factors (TFs) play a crucial role in driving cell differentiation by repressing the old gene expression program while activating new ones at bifurcation points.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific consensus.

claim: The balance between antagonistic TFs is a key determinant of cell fate, with the more highly expressed factor silencing the opposing factor.
source: The balance between antagonistic TFs is a key determinant of cell fate, with the more highly expressed factor silencing the opposing factor (Graf and Enver, 2009; Orkin and Zon, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Graf and Enver, 2009; Orkin and Zon, 2008.

claim: C/EBPα-induced transdifferentiation of B cells into macrophages is an especially efficient system for studying mechanisms of cell fate decisions.
source: An especially efficient system for this purpose is the C/EBPα-induced transdifferentiation of B cells into macrophages, designated here as BMT (Xie et al., 2004 ; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2004 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Post-translational modifications of TFs can have a significant impact on their structure, subcellular localization, interactions with other proteins and activity.
source: Post-translational modifications of TFs can have a significant impact on their structure, subcellular localization, interactions with other proteins and activity (Deribe et al., 2010; Torcal Garcia and Graf, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deribe et al., 2010; Torcal Garcia and Graf, 2021.

claim: Carm1 is crucial for early embryo development, muscle regeneration, adipogenesis, and cancer.
source: In the context of cell fate decisions, Carm1 (Prmt4) is of particular interest as it is crucial for early embryo development, muscle regeneration, adipogenesis, and cancer (Kawabe et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Torres-Padilla et al., 2007; Yadav et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Carm1-mediated methylation of a specific arginine located in the intrinsically disordered transcription activation domain of C/EBPα plays a critical role in regulating the speed of transdifferentiation induced by this factor.
source: Our study revealed that Carm1-mediated methylation of a specific arginine located in the intrinsically disordered transcription activation domain of C/EBPα plays a critical role in regulating the speed of transdifferentiation induced by this factor.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: In its mutated or unmethylated form C/EBPα induces BMT at a dramatically increased velocity, initiated by a higher interaction affinity for its partner TF PU.1.
source: In its mutated or unmethylated form C/EBPα induces BMT at a dramatically increased velocity, initiated by a higher interaction affinity for its partner TF PU.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental findings including Co-IP, mass spectrometry, and PLA data.

claim: The methyltransferase involved in the methylation of C/EBPa is Carm1, and it plays a role in determining the lineage directionality of GMPs.
source: The methyltransferase involved in the methylation of C/EBPa is Carm1, and it plays a role in determining the lineage directionality of GMPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro methylation assays and colony forming assays with GMPs.

claim: C/EBPα acts as a trigger for PU.1, which serves as a 'relay' that couples the concomitant silencing and activation of gene expression.
source: In this scenario, C/EBPα acts as a trigger for PU.1, which serves as a 'relay' that couples the concomitant silencing and activation of gene expression (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: The relay mechanism ensures the faithful establishment of the macrophage transcriptome and avoids the formation of 'confused' cells.
source: This mechanism avoids the formation of 'confused' cells, such as cells that upregulate the macrophage program without silencing the B cell program or vice versa, and therefore ensures the faithful establishment of the macrophage transcriptome.
evidence: This claim is a functional interpretation of the relay mechanism.

claim: PU.1 is expressed at approximately twice the levels in macrophages than in B cells.
source: Of note, we have not attempted to integrate into our model the fact that PU.1 is expressed at approximately twice the levels in macrophages than in B cells (Singh et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 1999.

claim: A mechanism similar to the C/EBPα-induced redistribution of PU.1 from B- to M-GREs has been described for Gata6-induced reprogramming of ESCs into primitive endoderm.
source: A mechanism similar to the C/EBPα-induced redistribution ('theft') of PU.1 from B- to M-GREs by an incoming TF as described here has recently been described for Gata6-induced reprogramming of ESCs into primitive endoderm (Thompson et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thompson et al., 2022.

claim: A theft mechanism involving PU.1 has been reported for T cell differentiation where PU.1 acts as the 'thief' by redirecting the Runx1 and Satb1 to novel sites.
source: A theft mechanism involving PU.1 has also been reported for T cell differentiation although in this case PU.1 acts as the 'thief' by redirecting the Runx1 and Satb1 to novel sites (Hosokawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hosokawa et al., 2018.

claim: Tbet sequesters Gata3 from Th2 genes and relocates it to Th1 genes during Th1 cell specification.
source: Another relevant example is the sequestering of Gata3 by Tbet from Th2 genes and its relocation to Th1 genes during Th1 cell specification (Hertweck et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hertweck et al., 2022.

claim: TF-mediated redistribution by a theft or 'relay' mechanism may be a more widespread phenomenon governing cell fate decisions during differentiation.
source: Thus, TF-mediated redistribution by a theft or 'relay' mechanism as proposed here may be a more widespread phenomenon governing cell fate decisions during differentiation.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the findings and comparison with other systems.

claim: R35 is methylated but not citrullinated in myeloid cells.
source: However, against this possibility is our previous finding that R35 is methylated but not citrullinated in myeloid cells (Ramberger et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramberger et al., 2021b.

claim: TP064 is a highly specific inhibitor of Carm1 that blocks the substrate binding site of the enzyme.
source: Another argument is the observed capacity of TP064 to accelerate BMT, as this is a highly specific inhibitor of Carm1 that blocks the substrate binding site of the enzyme (Nakayama et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakayama et al., 2018.

claim: C/EBPαWT can bind to closed chromatin and induce a transition to open chromatin.
source: Thus, while C/EBPαWT can bind to closed chromatin and induce a transition to open chromatin, the combination with PU.1 does so faster and this is even further accelerated with C/EBPαR35A, at speeds exceeding that of other pioneer TFs studied so far (Lerner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule tracking experiments and a citation to Lerner et al., 2020.

claim: The combination of C/EBPα with PU.1 induces chromatin opening faster than C/EBPαWT alone, and this is even further accelerated with C/EBPαR35A, at speeds exceeding that of other pioneer TFs studied so far.
source: Thus, while C/EBPαWT can bind to closed chromatin and induce a transition to open chromatin, the combination with PU.1 does so faster and this is even further accelerated with C/EBPαR35A, at speeds exceeding that of other pioneer TFs studied so far (Lerner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule tracking experiments and a citation to Lerner et al., 2020.

claim: Carm1-deficient mice are resistant to MLL-AF9-induced acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Thus, Carm1-deficient mice are resistant to MLL-AF9-induced acute myeloid leukemia (Greenblatt et al., 2016; Greenblatt et al., 2018), probably because a critical target protein cannot be methylated by the enzyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greenblatt et al., 2016; Greenblatt et al., 2018.

claim: C/EBPα is required for the formation of MLL-AF9-induced AML.
source: This target might be C/EBPα itself, which had been shown to be required for the formation of MLL-AF9-induced AML (Ye et al., 2015; Ohlsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ye et al., 2015; Ohlsson et al., 2016.

claim: In GMPs the methylated form of C/EBPα promotes the development of granulocytes, while the unmethylated form drives monocyte formation.
source: Our findings suggest that in GMPs the methylated form of C/EBPα promotes the development of granulocytes, while the unmethylated form drives monocyte formation, consistent with observations with the Carm1 knockout model (Greenblatt et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and is consistent with a citation to Greenblatt et al., 2018.

claim: Asymmetric di-methylation of four arginines in Pax7 results in the recruitment of MLL1/2, activation of Myf5 and subsequent muscle cell specification.
source: Here, asymmetric di-methylation of four arginines in Pax7 results in the recruitment of MLL1/2, activation of Myf5 and subsequent muscle cell specification (Chang et al., 2018; Kawabe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2018; Kawabe et al., 2012.

claim: The requirement of Carm1 for early embryo development has been associated with the methylation of H3R26 and BAF155.
source: Another example is the requirement of Carm1 for early embryo development, which has been associated with the methylation of H3R26 and BAF155 and have been proposed as drivers of the process (Torres-Padilla et al., 2007; Panamarova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Torres-Padilla et al., 2007; Panamarova et al., 2016.

claim: The balance of two forms of a single TF - one post-translationally modified and the other not - can determine the directionality of a binary cell fate decision.
source: Importantly, they suggest that the balance of two forms of a single TF - one post-translationally modified and the other not - can determine the directionality of a binary cell fate decision.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: This finding challenges the current view that the relative levels of antagonistic lineage-instructive TFs are primarily decisive for cell fate decisions.
source: This finding challenges the current view that the relative levels of antagonistic lineage-instructive TFs are primarily decisive for cell fate decisions (Radomska et al., 1998; Graf and Enver, 2009; Torcal Garcia and Graf, 2021).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and is contrasted with citations to Radomska et al., 1998; Graf and Enver, 2009; Torcal Garcia and Graf, 2021.

claim: Enzyme-mediated TF modifications that accelerate the speed of transdifferentiation may apply more broadly to cell fate decisions during development and differentiation.
source: Enzyme-mediated TF modifications that accelerate the speed of transdifferentiation, as described here, may apply more broadly to cell fate decisions during development and differentiation.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Chromatin remodeling can be uncoupled from gene expression during BMT.
source: It is also noteworthy that despite progressive alterations in chromatin accessibility at B- and M-GREs during BMT induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), essentially no changes in gene expression were observed between 6–18 hpi, suggesting that chromatin remodeling is uncoupled from gene expression during this phase of the process.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that chromatin accessibility changes occur without corresponding gene expression changes during a specific time window.

claim: C/EBPα and PU.1 can act as pioneer factors.
source: These findings support the observed ability of C/EBPα and PU.1 to interact with nucleosomes in vitro and to act as a pioneer factors (Fernandez Garcia et al., 2019; Lerner et al., 2020; van Oevelen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fernandez Garcia et al., 2019; Lerner et al., 2020; van Oevelen et al., 2015.
